video.title: Teaching debugging: A routine pupils can follow
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Sir, it doesn’t work! I hear it twenty times a lesson. If I fix every program myself, my pupils learn that bugs are my job. I want them to fix their own.
Today: how to teach debugging as a skill.
Start with the error message. Pupils often panic at the red text, but it’s a clue. Read the last line first: it names the problem. Then find the line number, and look there, and just above it.

Four errors cover most beginner bugs. SyntaxError: Python can’t read the line, often a missing colon or bracket. NameError: a name spelt differently. TypeError: text and a number mixed. IndexError: past the end of a list.
Then give pupils a routine. Read the error and find the line. Say what you expected, and what happened. Change one thing only. Run it again, and if it still fails, go back to step one.

The hardest bugs give no error at all. The program runs, and prints the wrong answer. Here, pupils add print lines to see the values as it runs, or trace it on paper. Compare what you expected with what you got.
Quick check! A pupil’s program stops with NameError: name scor isn’t defined. What is the most likely cause?
The spelling. The variable was made as score, but used as scor. Teach pupils to compare the name in the error with the line where the variable was made, letter by letter.

When a pupil calls you, don’t take the keyboard. Ask questions instead. What did you expect? What does the error say? What is x after line two? The pupil finds the bug, and learns how to find the next one.
One more trick: rubber duck debugging. Pupils explain their program, line by line, out loud, to a toy, a partner or the wall. Halfway through, they often hear the mistake themselves.
In the app, open Bug hunt. Six programs, six common bugs. Run each one before fixing it, read the error aloud, and notice that bug three gives no error at all: it just prints the wrong thing.
Your turn. A pupil’s loop prints the wrong total, with no error. What is the best thing to say first?

Ask what total should be. Remember: an error message is a clue; read the last line and the line number. Follow a routine: read, expect, change one thing, run again. Ask questions instead of fixing. And bugs with no error need tracing.
Try it in class tomorrow: bug of the day. Start each lesson this week with a short program on the board that has one bug. Pupils find it in pairs, and say how they found it, not just what it was.

checkpoints.prompt: NameError: name 'scor' isn’t defined. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The name is spelt differently from where it was made

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the variable was made as score, and line 3 asks for scor.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a NameError means Python doesn’t know the name: usually a spelling or capital-letter slip.

checkpoints.prompt: A pupil’s loop prints the wrong total, with no error. What is the best thing to say first?

options.text: “Line 3 is wrong; write it like this.”
“What should total be after the first time round?”

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a question sends the pupil back to trace their own program.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — giving the fix solves this bug, not the next one. Ask a question that makes them trace.
